metadata.note: The Chicago 'L' -- every rapid transit line the city has had, from the South Side Rapid Transit's steam-hauled elevated of June 6 1892 to today's eight colour-coded CTA routes, together with the branches that did not survive. Four private companies built the system between 1892 and 1900 -- the Chicago and South Side Rapid Transit (renamed the South Side Elevated Railroad in 1897), the Lake Street Elevated, the Metropolitan West Side Elevated (the first electric elevated railroad in the United States, May 6 1895) and the Northwestern Elevated -- each running into its own stub terminal on the edge of downtown until Charles Yerkes's Union Elevated Railroad tied them together with the Union Loop, completed September 6 1897. The Chicago Elevated Railways trust of July 1 1911 unified their management and brought free transfers and through routing; on January 9 1924 the four companies were formally merged into Samuel Insull's Chicago Rapid Transit Company, which added the Niles Center and Westchester branches, opened the State Street subway in 1943, and went bankrupt. The Chicago Transit Authority took over on October 1 1947 and spent the next fifteen years pruning: Niles Center 1948, Westchester 1951, Humboldt Park 1952, Normal Park 1954, Stock Yards and Kenwood 1957, and the Garfield Park elevated in 1958, replaced by the Congress Expressway median -- the first rapid transit line in the world laid in an expressway median. Growth resumed with the Skokie Swift (1964), the Dan Ryan branch (1969), the Kennedy median to Jefferson Park (1970) and O'Hare (1984), the Orange Line to Midway (1993) and the Pink Line over the rebuilt Paulina Connector (2006). STRUCTURE: because CLAUDE.md Rule 4 requires one colour per company and a feature split at every ownership change, each corridor appears once per operator -- the original company to January 1924, the Chicago Rapid Transit Company 1924-1947, and the CTA from October 1947 -- with identical geometry and the new owner's colour. The pre-1947 private companies are drawn as mode 'elevated_rail' and the CTA network as 'rapid_transit', matching how cities/new_york_elevated.geojson and cities/new_york_subway.geojson split the two. Every CTA feature carries ONE colour: the Red Line is not drawn red. The branding is in the line name, as Rule 4 requires for modern transit agencies. GEOMETRY: modern lines are the OSM route relations for each CTA service, walked in member order; historic corridors are the OSM ways the CTA still owns, taken as a single-track spine (the double-sweep path through a graph of the named ways) so that the two tracks of a double-track line are not drawn as an out-and-back spike; the Kenwood, Stock Yards, East 63rd and outer Douglas branches come from OSM railway=abandoned/razed ways still on the ground. Five lines have no surviving mapped structure and are drawn as labelled straight-line approximations along the streets they ran above -- see each feature's geometry_quality.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: HEADWAYS AND SPEEDS ARE ESTIMATES. No timetable research was done for any feature: every headway_min is a plausible round number for the era and the service type, and every avg_speed_kmh is a guess at schedule speed including station stops. Do not read them as sourced. DATE CONFLICT: the South Side Elevated article dates the Jackson Park extension May 12 1893, the Green Line article May 1 1893; the Union Loop is given as September 6 1897 by the Loop article and as October 3 1897 by several other accounts; the Metropolitan's opening is May 6 1895 in the Logan Square and Blue Line articles and May 7 1895 in the Metropolitan article. The earlier date is used in each case and the conflict is recorded here rather than resolved. The Chicago Elevated Railways trust is dated July 1 1911 by the Logan Square article and 1913 by the Northwestern Elevated article; because the trust kept the underlying companies intact it is treated here as a management change, not an ownership change, and no feature is split at it -- the split is at the formal CRT merger of January 9 1924. GEOMETRY: the Garfield Park branch, the Metropolitan main line, the Normal Park branch, the Humboldt Park branch, the Westchester branch south of Bellwood and the southern half of the Logan Square branch have no surviving mapped structure and are drawn as straight-line street approximations; each says so in its geometry_quality and none should be trusted to better than a city block. The Lake Street branch west of Laramie is drawn on the post-1962 C&NW embankment even for the years it ran in the middle of South Boulevard, and the Garfield Park branch is drawn partly on the 1958 Congress median that replaced it. The Stock Yards branch's counterclockwise loop through the packing plants is not in OSM, so 2.13 of its documented 2.9 mi are drawn. Station locations are not modelled anywhere in this file. OPEN QUESTION: the year the Lake Street 'L' was cut back from Marengo Avenue, Forest Park to Harlem Avenue is not established here, so the Lake Street features are drawn only as far west as Harlem.
